extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and academic researchers who must write letters of recommendation, book reviews, referee reports, and research talks
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing professional academic materials: letters of recommendation (for faculty and students), mathematical book reviews, referee reports for journals, and research talks. Focuses on what to include, how to phrase judgments, and common pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague praise; be specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write vague, generic praise (e.g., 'Give him whatever he wants'); such letters say nothing and can be construed as faint praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dwell for a page or more on specific virtues. Vague letters are dangerous because they can be misread; specificity forces clarity and is hard to misconstrue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give detailed remarks about specific papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Make detailed remarks about specific papers: why the result is important, how it improves on earlier work, and how it advances the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide background and motivation for nonspecialist readers, mention who else has worked on the problem, and cite publication venues (e.g., Annals, Inventiones) to signal quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use binary comparisons to peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the candidate to other people of similar age and career level (preferably recognizable academic mathematicians) to place the candidate in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit comparisons (e.g., 'the five best people under 35 are A,B,C,D,E' or 'Candidate fits between Jones and Schmones') are persuasive. Be concrete: a rank or relative placement is better than silence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor comparisons to the audience and circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust comparisons to the institution and to what the soliciting letter asks for; avoid inappropriate comparisons (e.g., a recent Ph.D. vs a senior NAS member).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If solicited by a teaching-focused college, emphasize teaching, curriculum, and appropriate publication venues rather than deep research comparisons. Read the solicitation carefully and 'speak their language.'

rubrics_metrics.name: State a clear, explicit recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Answer the question posed (tenure, promotion, hire) point blank; do not be evasive or neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You are expected to render an opinion. Use explicit, forceful language when warranted ('I recommend X enthusiastically', 'I recommend without reservation'). Avoid ambiguous closing lines that readers interpret negatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid self-serving diversion to your own work
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not spend the letter describing the writer's own work or how the candidate's theorem is based on the writer's ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such tangents mark the writer as self-absorbed and do nothing to help the candidate. Keep focus on the candidate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid equivocal or lukewarm phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases that sound positive but are weak (e.g., 'warmly' read as 'lukewarm') can be damaging; weak praise can be interpreted as negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives a graded list of sample closings and notes how readers will interpret each; aim for words that convey genuine enthusiasm when you mean to support the candidate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not gratuitously demean other institutions or audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements like 'not good enough for us but good enough for you' insult many people and render the letter ineffectual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you must contextualize a difference in standards, do so respectfully (e.g., explain Harvard's unusually high bar and recommend for an appropriate comparable institution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize teaching, talks, and collaboration where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Mention whether the candidate gives excellent talks, is a good collaborator, and any credible evidence of teaching effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are not in the candidate's department, rely on colleagues' testimony where appropriate; a knowledgeable comment on teaching can make a strong impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: For student letters: be specific; avoid most binary comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Students often lack publications and peer comparisons; instead provide concrete, memorable examples of the student's abilities (class performance, original proofs, problems posed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Say things like 'one of the five most talented undergraduates I've taught' or describe particular achievements; avoid absurd cross-generational comparisons unless genuinely appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you cannot write a good/supportive letter, decline
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have nothing positive to say or feel you cannot write a supportive letter, tell the candidate rather than agreeing and failing to produce a useful letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A missing letter can render a dossier incomplete; be honest and give the candidate the courtesy of a 'pass' if you cannot help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisor and external letters for fresh Ph.D. should be detailed and informative
rubrics_metrics.description: A meat-and-potatoes job dossier should include a detailed thesis-advisor letter and additional letters that add substantive information rather than repeating the advisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convince other writers to know something about the thesis; obtain at least one external letter if possible and ensure teaching abilities are addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest and preserve your credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistent overpraise or dishonest letters will damage your long-term credibility as a letter writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call it as you see it; a reputation for making tough decisions will make your letters count. The infrastructure 'remembers' letter writers' tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address English fluency honestly and precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid formulaic or overstated claims about a candidate's spoken English; instead give concrete evidence (teaching experience, progress, intelligibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide nuanced phrasing (from 'speaks like a home-grown American' to 'has made substantial progress but requires concentration to understand') depending on reality; implicit evidence (e.g., excellent teaching) can also speak to fluency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention personal matters only when relevant to job performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitive personal facts (e.g., gender transition) should be considered for mention only if they materially affect teaching or collegial functioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully weigh relevance and consult mentors; do not gratuitously mention private matters that do not impact job performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book review: write an essay about the subject, not a chapter-by-chapter report
rubrics_metrics.description: A book review should place the book within the broader subject area, discussing history, milestones, major players, and big problems before focusing on the book itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the book as an occasion to write about the field (à la New York Review of Books); but remember the review must still serve the reader deciding whether to read/buy the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book review: evaluate pedagogical and reference features
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether students will benefit, whether exercises, lists of open problems, bibliography, index, and notation lists are present and adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the starting level, sufficiency of review material, and how navigable the book is for beginners or the intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book review: assess technical completeness and organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether the author provides adequate detail, whether proofs are complete/clear/accurate, whether the book is well organized, and whether it brings the reader to the cutting edge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out omissions, errors, or places needing improvement; balance criticism with charity so the review is useful and dignified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book review: be constructive and avoid personal vitriol
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms should be candid but constructive and scholarly; avoid personal attacks, excessive venom, or letting anger obscure useful points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If tempted to trash a book, set the draft aside (e.g., a month), let it mellow, show it to trusted colleagues, and revise to a more tempered and useful critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee's report: be timely
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit the referee's report within the journal's suggested timeframe when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness is part of professional duty; indicate if more time is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee's report: state and defend your opinion clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Enunciate your opinion succinctly, defend it in detail, and summarize the findings; make a specific recommendation (accept/revise/reject).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recommendation is the most important part; supporting commentary is for the record. Typical reports run 1–5 pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee's report: read enough to judge correctness, novelty, and surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: You need not check every detail, but you must read enough to be confident of the paper's correctness, importance, and novelty (Littlewood's three precepts: Is it new? Is it correct? Is it surprising?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speak to the paper's contribution to knowledge and literature; do not issue a report without being confident of your assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee's report: provide constructive criticisms of content and exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Point out mathematical errors, unclear reasoning, organizational problems, and, if desired, spelling/grammatical issues—but avoid captiousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be helpful: focus on items that affect understanding and correctness. Provide suggestions where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee's report: place the paper in context and tailor to the journal
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how the paper compares to recent work, where it fits in the literature, and whether it meets the journal's standards and aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different journals have different missions (Annals vs more modest journals); judge the paper by the appropriate value system and language the editors/readers will understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Giving a talk: exploit informality but respect the medium's limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Talks can be more informal, include examples, and admit a bit of imprecision, but the audience receives content linearly and cannot rewind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete/trivial examples and describe things tried and failed to build intuition; be gentle and make the talk accessible so the linear delivery doesn't lose the audience.
